stem: A two-owner business expects losses for several years, wants to allocate most depreciation to one owner, and plans to bring in a corporate investor. Which entity best fits?

choices.explanation: No corporate owners and no special allocations.
Correct. Partnerships allow corporate partners, special allocations, and pass-through losses.

explanation: Partnerships allow corporate partners, special allocations, and pass-through losses.

stem: A single-member LLC owned by a C corporation makes no election. How is it treated?

choices.text: As an S corporation owned by the parent
choices.explanation: A corporation can't own an S corporation's stock (except a QSub).

choices.text: As a partnership with the parent
choices.explanation: A partnership needs two or more owners.

choices.text: As a disregarded division of the parent
choices.explanation: Correct. Single-owner eligible entities default to disregarded status.

explanation: Single-owner eligible entities default to disregarded status.

stem: Which statement about the §199A QBI deduction in entity planning is correct?

choices.text: It is available to C corporations on their taxable income
It applies to wages that an S corporation pays its owner
It can cut the top rate on pass-through income to 29.6%
It expired for tax years beginning after 2025
choices.explanation: It was made permanent by P.L. 119-21.

stem: In a §351 exchange, D transfers property (basis $30,000; FMV $80,000) subject to a $50,000 liability for stock. The corporation assumes the liability. What gain does D recognize and what is her stock basis?

choices.explanation: Only the excess over basis is gain.

stem: A shareholder's $70,000 loss on the sale of §1244 stock is reported by a single taxpayer. How is it treated?

choices.explanation: Correct. §1244(b): ordinary loss up to $50,000 for single filers; the excess is capital.

explanation: §1244(b): ordinary loss up to $50,000 for single filers; the excess is capital.

stem: After a redemption, a shareholder owns 45% of the voting stock, down from 55%. No attribution applies. How is the redemption treated?

choices.text: A §301 distribution unless another test is met
choices.explanation: Correct. Needs < 50% AND < 44%; 45% fails the 80% test.

explanation: Needs < 50% AND < 44%; 45% fails the 80% test.

stem: In a §332 liquidation of a 100% subsidiary, the subsidiary has a $1 million NOL. What happens to the NOL?

choices.text: It is refunded to the parent
It carries over to the parent, with limits
choices.explanation: Correct. §381 carries over tax attributes in a §332 liquidation.

choices.text: It must be used by the shareholders
choices.explanation: Attributes go to the parent corporation.

explanation: §381 carries over tax attributes in a §332 liquidation.

stem: Company Q's only presence in State R is an employee who performs repairs on products sold to State R customers. Can State R impose its net income tax on Q?

choices.text: Only if Q's sales there exceed $500,000
choices.explanation: Economic thresholds aren't needed with physical presence.

choices.text: No, because one employee can't create nexus
choices.explanation: Physical presence of an employee creates nexus.

explanation: Non-solicitation activities remove P.L. 86-272 protection.

stem: A company's State T factors: sales 10%, property 40%, payroll 30%. State T switches from an equally weighted three-factor formula to a single sales factor. By how many percentage points does the company's State T apportionment change?

choices.explanation: Uses the property factor as the baseline.

stem: Which income is most likely allocated rather than apportioned?

choices.text: Gross receipts from sales of inventory

choices.explanation: Working capital interest is usually business income.

choices.text: Rent from an unrelated investment lot
choices.explanation: Correct. Nonbusiness income, like rent on unrelated investment property, is allocated.

explanation: Nonbusiness income, like rent on unrelated investment property, is allocated.

stem: Equipment (cost $50,000; depreciation $50,000, all bonus) is sold for $60,000 after 3 years. What is the character of the gain?
explanation: Basis 0; gain 60,000; recapture 50,000.

stem: An individual's net §1231 gain is $25,000 for 2025. Net §1231 losses were $(10,000) in 2019 and $(8,000) in 2022, with no gains since. How much is ordinary?

choices.explanation: The 2019 loss is outside the 5-year lookback.
Correct. Only losses from the 5 preceding years (2020–2024) count, so the 2019 loss is excluded: 8,000.

explanation: Only losses from the 5 preceding years (2020–2024) count, so the 2019 loss is excluded: 8,000.

stem: A C corporation sells a warehouse (straight-line depreciation $300,000) at a $500,000 gain. How much is ordinary income under §291?
An individual sells land (basis $90,000) for $300,000: $60,000 down in 2025 and $240,000 in 2027. No liabilities. How much gain is recognized in 2025?
In a §1031 exchange, E gives property (basis $200,000; FMV $500,000) and $40,000 cash for property worth $540,000. What is E's recognized gain and new basis?
explanation: No boot received; basis = 200,000 + 40,000.

stem: A father sells land (basis $100,000) to his daughter for $70,000. She later sells it for $90,000. What is her recognized gain?

choices.explanation: The disallowed loss offsets her gain.
Correct. §267(d): her 20,000 gain is reduced by the father's 30,000 disallowed loss (not below zero).
Her gain can't become a loss.

explanation: §267(d): her 20,000 gain is reduced by the father's 30,000 disallowed loss (not below zero).

stem: Which transaction can use the installment method?

choices.text: An individual's sale of a rental building, paid over 10 years
choices.explanation: Correct. Non-dealer sales of real property qualify.

choices.text: A dealer's sale of subdivided lots
A sale of publicly traded stock
Sale of depreciable property to a 60%-owned corporation
choices.explanation: §453(g) bars it for related depreciable property.

explanation: Non-dealer sales of real property qualify.

stem: A business sells machinery (cost $70,000; accumulated depreciation $45,000) for $30,000. What is the character of the gain?

choices.explanation: Recapture is limited to the gain.

stem: What is the maximum federal rate on unrecaptured §1250 gain for an individual?

choices.explanation: Unrecaptured §1250 gain has a higher cap.
Correct. Unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at a maximum of 25%.

explanation: Unrecaptured §1250 gain is taxed at a maximum of 25%.

stem: In a like-kind exchange, a taxpayer gives real property (basis $80,000; FMV $150,000) and receives real property (FMV $140,000) plus $10,000 cash. What gain is recognized?

choices.explanation: Correct. Recognized gain = lesser of realized 70,000 or boot 10,000.

explanation: Recognized gain = lesser of realized 70,000 or boot 10,000.

stem: Which property can qualify for a §1031 like-kind exchange in 2025?

choices.explanation: Correct. Only real property held for business or investment qualifies.
Not held for business or investment.
Property held for sale is excluded.

explanation: Only real property held for business or investment qualifies.

stem: A corporation has accumulated E&P of $10,000 and current E&P of $25,000. It distributes $50,000 to its sole shareholder (basis $40,000). What is the dividend?

choices.explanation: Correct. Dividend = 25,000 current + 10,000 accumulated = 35,000; 15,000 reduces basis.

explanation: Dividend = 25,000 current + 10,000 accumulated = 35,000; 15,000 reduces basis.

stem: A corporation distributes land (FMV $60,000; basis $20,000) to a shareholder. What gain does the corporation recognize?

choices.explanation: Gain is recognized on appreciated property.
That's the property's basis, not the gain.
Correct. §311(b): recognize gain as if sold.

explanation: §311(b): recognize gain as if sold.

stem: Which is most likely treated as a constructive dividend?

choices.text: Reasonable salary paid to a shareholder-employee
A corporation's payment of a shareholder's personal vacation
choices.explanation: Correct. Payments of shareholders' personal expenses are constructive dividends.

choices.text: Repayment of a bona fide loan from a shareholder
Rent paid to a shareholder at fair market rates

explanation: Payments of shareholders' personal expenses are constructive dividends.

stem: In a §351 exchange, a shareholder transfers property (basis $60,000; FMV $100,000) for stock worth $90,000 and $10,000 cash. What is her stock basis?
A shareholder owns 30% of a corporation; after a redemption she owns 20%. No attribution applies. Is the redemption substantially disproportionate?

choices.text: Yes; she owns under 50% and under 80% of 30%
No, because she still owns some stock
choices.explanation: Complete termination isn't required for this test.

choices.text: No, because she must own less than 10%

stem: A parent corporation owning 100% of a subsidiary receives the subsidiary's assets in a complete liquidation. What is the parent's basis in those assets?

choices.explanation: Correct. §332/§334(b): no gain or loss; carryover basis.
The parent takes the subsidiary's basis.

explanation: §332/§334(b): no gain or loss; carryover basis.

stem: An owner-operator's business earns $200,000. Compared with operating as a single-member LLC, electing S corporation status mainly reduces:

choices.text: Income tax, because S income is tax-exempt
choices.explanation: S income passes through and is taxed.

choices.text: Employment taxes on profit above a reasonable salary
choices.explanation: Correct. S distributions above reasonable compensation aren't subject to payroll taxes.

choices.text: Payroll tax on the owner's reasonable salary
choices.explanation: Reasonable salary is subject to FICA.

choices.text: Tax on capital gains from a later sale of the business
choices.explanation: The election mainly affects employment taxes.

explanation: An S shareholder-employee pays FICA on reasonable compensation; remaining profit flows through without self-employment tax, unlike an LLC member.

stem: Which business owner is not eligible for the §199A qualified business income deduction on that business's income?

choices.text: A partner in a manufacturing partnership
The sole shareholder of a C corporation
choices.explanation: Correct. QBI applies to pass-through income, not C corporations.

choices.text: A sole proprietor with a retail store
choices.explanation: Schedule C income can be QBI.

explanation: IRC §199A allows the deduction for qualified business income from sole proprietorships, partnerships and S corporations, not C corporations.

stem: In a §351 exchange, a shareholder transfers property (basis $40,000; fair value $100,000) subject to a $55,000 liability the corporation assumes. No boot is received. What gain does the shareholder recognize?

choices.explanation: Liabilities in excess of basis trigger gain.
Only the excess over basis is gain.
Realized gain is recognized only to the extent of the excess liability.
Correct. §357(c): liabilities exceeding basis by 15,000 create gain.

explanation: IRC §357(c): in a §351 exchange, liabilities assumed in excess of the transferor's basis produce gain.

stem: A parent owning 90% of a subsidiary liquidates the subsidiary. Under §332, the parent:

choices.text: No gain; carryover basis in the assets
choices.explanation: Correct. A qualifying parent-subsidiary liquidation is tax-free to the parent.

choices.text: Recognizes gain on the subsidiary's assets
Takes a fair value basis in the assets

explanation: IRC §332, §334(b): a corporation owning at least 80% recognizes no gain or loss in its subsidiary's liquidation and takes carryover basis.

stem: For sales of services, most states now source receipts for the sales factor to:

choices.text: The state where the seller incurs most of its costs
choices.explanation: That is the older cost-of-performance rule.

choices.text: The state where the customer receives the benefit
choices.explanation: Correct. Market-based sourcing is now the majority rule.

choices.text: The state where the contract is signed

explanation: Most states have moved from cost-of-performance to market-based sourcing for services and intangibles.

stem: Equipment cost $100,000, has $60,000 of accumulated depreciation and is sold for $70,000. How is the gain characterized?

choices.explanation: Recapture is limited to the gain.
Correct. All gain up to depreciation taken is recaptured as ordinary.

explanation: IRC §1245: gain on depreciable personal property is ordinary to the extent of depreciation taken; any excess is §1231 gain.

stem: A C corporation sells a building for a $200,000 gain; it took $150,000 of straight-line depreciation. How much is ordinary income under §291?

choices.explanation: Correct. 20% × the lesser of the gain or the straight-line depreciation (150,000).

explanation: IRC §291(a)(1): a corporation treats 20% of the excess of what would be §1245 recapture over §1250 recapture as ordinary income.

stem: A taxpayer sells investment land (basis $200,000) for $500,000: $100,000 down in 2025 and the rest in later years, with adequate interest. How much gain is recognized in 2025 under the installment method?

choices.explanation: Only the gross profit portion of the payment is gain.
That is the return of basis portion.

explanation: IRC §453: gain recognized = payments received × gross profit ratio.

stem: In a like-kind exchange of real property, a taxpayer gives property worth $300,000 (basis $180,000) and receives property worth $260,000 plus $40,000 cash. What gain is recognized, and what is the basis of the new property?

choices.explanation: Correct. Gain is the lesser of realized gain (120,000) or boot (40,000); basis = 180,000 + 40,000 − 40,000.

explanation: IRC §1031: recognized gain = lesser of realized gain or boot received; new basis = old basis + gain recognized − boot received.

stem: A C corporation earns $100,000 and distributes all of its after-tax income as a qualified dividend to a shareholder taxed at 20% on dividends. Ignoring the NIIT, what is the combined tax?
explanation: Double taxation: 21% at the corporate level, then the shareholder's dividend rate on the after-tax distribution.

stem: Gwen owns 60 of 100 shares of a corporation (no attribution). The corporation redeems 30 of her shares. Does the redemption qualify as substantially disproportionate under §302(b)(2)?

choices.text: No; she still owns more than 40%
choices.explanation: The test is 80% of prior ownership and under 50%.

choices.text: No; she remains the largest shareholder
Yes; any redemption of half the shares qualifies
choices.explanation: The percentage tests must be met.

choices.text: Yes; she owns 42.9%, under 48% and under 50%
choices.explanation: Correct. 30 ÷ 70 = 42.9%, which is below 80% of 60% (48%) and below 50%.

explanation: IRC §302(b)(2): after the redemption the shareholder must own less than 50% of voting stock and less than 80% of her prior percentage.

stem: In a §331 complete liquidation, a shareholder with a stock basis of $60,000 receives property worth $150,000. What does the shareholder recognize?

choices.explanation: Correct. Liquidating distributions are treated as payment in exchange for the stock.

choices.text: No gain until the property is sold
choices.explanation: Gain is recognized on the liquidation.

explanation: IRC §331: amounts received in complete liquidation are full payment for the stock; gain is capital, and basis in the property is fair value.

stem: A corporation distributes appreciated land to shareholders in a complete liquidation. The corporation:

choices.text: Recognizes no gain because shareholders pay tax
choices.explanation: Both levels are taxed in a §331/§336 liquidation.

choices.text: Recognizes gain as if it sold the land
choices.explanation: Correct. §336 treats liquidating distributions as sales.

choices.text: Defers gain until the shareholders sell
Recognizes gain only if the land is inventory

explanation: IRC §336(a): a liquidating corporation recognizes gain or loss as if it sold distributed property at fair value (with some loss limits).

stem: Under combined (unitary) reporting, a state taxes a multistate group by:

choices.text: Taxing each subsidiary separately, ignoring affiliates
Allocating all income to the parent's domicile
Apportioning the unitary group's combined income
choices.explanation: Correct. Members of a unitary business compute and apportion income as a group.

choices.text: Exempting intercompany sales from the sales factor
choices.explanation: That is a feature, not the method itself.

explanation: Combined reporting treats related corporations engaged in a unitary business as one, apportioning combined income with combined factors.

stem: A business has a 2025 net §1231 gain of $50,000. It had $20,000 of net §1231 losses in 2022 that haven't been recaptured. How is the 2025 gain treated?

choices.explanation: Correct. The five-year lookback recaptures prior net §1231 losses.
Prior unrecaptured losses must be recaptured.
Only the lookback amount is ordinary.

explanation: IRC §1231(c): net §1231 gain is ordinary to the extent of nonrecaptured net §1231 losses of the prior five years.

stem: An individual sells a rental building for a $150,000 gain; he took $90,000 of straight-line depreciation. How much is unrecaptured §1250 gain taxed at up to 25%?

choices.explanation: Only the depreciation portion is unrecaptured §1250 gain.
Correct. Gain up to straight-line depreciation is unrecaptured §1250 gain.
Straight-line depreciation still creates unrecaptured §1250 gain.

explanation: IRC §1(h)(6): unrecaptured §1250 gain (gain attributable to straight-line depreciation on real property) is taxed at a maximum 25% for individuals.

stem: A business's warehouse (not condemned) is destroyed by fire in 2025, and insurance proceeds exceed basis. Within what period must it buy qualified replacement property to defer the gain under §1033?

choices.explanation: 180 days is a like-kind exchange deadline.
The period is two years after year-end.

choices.text: Five years after the end of the tax year
Two years after that tax year ends
choices.explanation: Correct. The general replacement period is two years (three for condemned business real property).

explanation: IRC §1033(a)(2)(B): replacement must occur within two years after the close of the first tax year in which any gain is realized (three years for condemned real property held for business or investment).

stem: Two brothers exchange like-kind real property. Eighteen months later, one brother sells the property he received. What happens?

choices.text: Only the selling brother recognizes gain
Both recognize their deferred gain that year
choices.explanation: Correct. §1031(f) requires related parties to hold for two years.

choices.text: Nothing; the exchange was already complete
The original exchange is amended retroactively
choices.explanation: Gain is recognized in the year of the disposition.

explanation: IRC §1031(f): if either related party disposes of the property within two years, the deferred gain is recognized as of the date of that disposition.

stem: Equipment with $25,000 of §1245 recapture is sold on the installment method for a $40,000 total gain. How much gain is recognized in the year of sale, before applying the gross profit ratio to the remaining gain?

choices.explanation: Correct. Depreciation recapture is recognized in the year of sale regardless of payments.

explanation: IRC §453(i): recapture income is recognized in the year of disposition; the remaining gain is reported under the installment method.
